en: "Those who give cows that have drunk their water, eaten their grass, had their milk milked, and are barren—devoid of strength and joy—go to those worlds called 'Joyless' (ananda). 1.3.
He said to his father, "Father, to whom will you give me? A second time and a third time he asked this. He said to him, "I give you to Death. 1.4.
"I go as the first among many; I go as the middlemost among many.
What indeed is this duty of Yama that he will perform through me today? (1.5)
Observe how it was for those of old, and observe likewise for those who come after;
like grain, a mortal ripens, and like grain, he is born again. (1.6)
The Vaiśvānara fire enters the house as a Brāhmaṇa guest; for him they perform this rite of pacification: "O Vaivasvata, carry away water! (1.7)
Hope, expectation, union, pleasant speech, the merit of sacrifices and public works, sons, and all cattle—
these take away from a man of small intelligence.
In whose house a Brahmin dwells without eating. || 1.8 ||
Since for three nights you have stayed in my house as a guest, O Brahmin, without eating— you who are worthy of honor—
homage be to you, O Brahmin; may it be well with me.
Therefore, choose three boons for yourself. || 1.9 ||
O Death, may Gautama be one whose intentions are peaceful, well-disposed, and free from anger toward me; may he, being satisfied,
speak to me when released by you.
Of these three, I choose this first boon.
Just as in the past,
Uddālaka Āruṇi, sent forth by me, became renowned and free from resentment; so shall he sleep peacefully through the nights, his anger gone.
I have seen you released from the jaws of death.
In the heavenly world there is no fear whatsoever; neither you nor old age cause one to tremble there.
Having crossed over both hunger and thirst, one dwells there.
Having transcended sorrow, he rejoices in the heavenly world. || 1.12 ||
O Death, you know that Agni who leads to heaven; tell him to me, who am full of faith.
Those in the heavenly world partake of immortality.
This I choose with my second boon. || 1.13 ||
I declare this to you; understand it from me, O Naciketas, as I know it: the fire that leads to heaven, which secures the attainment of the infinite world and provides a firm foundation.
Know that this is hidden within the cave of the heart.
He spoke to him concerning that Agni, the beginning of the worlds—
what bricks there are, how many there are, and how they are arranged; and he (the disciple) replied to him exactly as it had been told.
Then Death, being pleased, spoke to him again.
The high-souled one, being pleased, said to him:
"I grant you yet another boon here today;
this fire shall be known by your very name."
And take this amulet of manifold forms.
One who has performed the Nāciketa fire-sacrifice thrice, having attained union by means of the three,
and who performs the three duties, transcends birth and death after knowing the God, the source of Brahman, the one worthy of praise.
Having realized this, one attains ultimate peace. || 1.17 ||
O Triṇāciketa, he who, having known this triad, being thus wise, builds the Nāciketa fire-altar— he,
having cast away the bonds of death before him, [attains immortality].
Having transcended sorrow, he rejoices in the heavenly world.
This is that heavenly fire for you, O Naciketas,
which you chose with your second boon;
people shall call this very fire by your name alone.
Choose a third boon, O Naciketas.
Regarding this doubt concerning a person after death—
some say "he exists," while others say "he does not exist"—
may I, instructed by you, come to know this.
This is the third boon among boons. || 1.20 ||
Even the gods had doubts about this in the past, for this Dharma is not easily understood; it is subtle.
Choose another boon, Naciketas.
Do not obstruct me; release him for me. 1.21.
Even the gods, it is said, were once in doubt regarding this matter, O Death, which you have declared to be so difficult to understand;
for another speaker like you cannot be found.
There is no other boon whatsoever that is equal to this.
Choose sons and grandsons who live for a hundred years;
choose many cattle, elephants, gold, and horses;
choose a vast expanse of land.
And you yourself shall live for as many autumns as you desire.
If you consider this equal [to that], choose a boon— wealth and long life—
and become a lord upon the great earth, O Naciketas.
I make you a partaker of desires. || 1.24 ||
Whatever desires are difficult to obtain in the world of mortals,
ask for all those desires according to your wish;
here are these beautiful women with their chariots and musical instruments.
"Indeed, such things as these are not to be obtained by mere mortals. Enjoy them with these gifts bestowed by me; O Naciketas, do not inquire about death. (1.25)
The future of mortals is tomorrow; this end, O Death, wears away the vigor of all the senses.
Even the entirety of life is indeed very short.
Your very mounts are yours; so too are your dance and song.
A man cannot be satisfied with wealth;
we would have obtained wealth had we seen you [before].
We shall live as long as you shall rule.
But he alone is the bridegroom who is worthy of my choice.
Having approached those who do not age and are immortal,
what shall the aging mortal— who stands below, knowing [this],
and reflecting upon the pleasures of color, taste, and delight— do?
Who would take delight in a life that is excessively long? 1.28.
O Death, tell us that about which they have doubts regarding the great hereafter;
this boon which has entered into the secret— tell us that.
Therefore, Naciketas chooses nothing else than that. 1.29.
Thus ends the first chapter.
The beneficial is one thing, and the pleasant is indeed another;
these two, having different aims, bind a person.
Of these two, for him who takes up the beneficial, it becomes well.
He who chooses that which is pleasant loses what is beneficial. 2.1.
The wise man, having fully circled around both the beneficial and the pleasant, distinguishes between them;
for the wise man chooses the beneficial over the pleasant.
The dull-witted man chooses what is pleasant over security and well-being. 2.2.
O Naciketas, you have renounced beloved objects of desire that appear attractive, even while longing for them;
you have not accepted this bait consisting of wealth.
In which many people sink. || 2.3 ||
Far apart, divergent, and leading in opposite directions are these two:
that which is known as ignorance and that which is known as knowledge. I consider Naciketas to be one who desires knowledge.
But many desires did not entice you. || 2.4 ||
Existing in the midst of ignorance,
yet considering themselves wise and learned,
the deluded wander about, running hither and thither.
Just as the blind are led by one who is himself blind. || 2.5 ||
The world beyond does not appear to the fool who is heedless, deluded by the infatuation for wealth,
and who thinks, "This world exists, but there is no other."
Again and again, he falls under my power. || 2.6 ||
He who is not obtained even for hearing by many,
whom many, though hearing, do not know— wonderful is the speaker, and skillful is the one who has found him.
He is wonderful, a knower, and well-instructed in what is wholesome. || 2.7 ||
This is not easily understood when proclaimed by an inferior person, for it is conceived in many ways;
there is no way to reach it unless it is proclaimed by one who is non-different [from the Truth].
For it is subtler than the subtle, beyond the reach of thought, and smaller in measure than an atom.
This wisdom is not to be attained by reasoning; it must be declared by another for the sake of right knowledge, O dearest one— wisdom which you have attained, for you are indeed steadfast in truth.
May one like you be even dearer to us than Naciketas. || 2.9 ||
I know that this treasure is impermanent;
for the eternal cannot be attained by means of things that are transient.
Therefore, the Nāciketa fire has been piled by me.
Through impermanent substances, I have attained the eternal.

Having beheld the fulfillment of desire, the foundation of the world, the infinity of sacrifice, the further shore of fearlessness, the great hymn of praise, and the wide-striding one as the ultimate support;
By means of fortitude, O wise Naciketas, you have transcended [all things]. || 2.11 ||
That ancient God, difficult to perceive, hidden, entered into the secret cave, dwelling in the abyss— [one perceives Him] through the attainment of the yoga of the supreme self.
Having understood this, the wise man abandons both joy and sorrow. || 2.12 ||
Having heard this and fully grasped it, a mortal who has extracted this subtle, righteous essence and attained it,
rejoices, for he has obtained that which is worthy of joy.
I consider the abode of Naciketas to have been revealed.
Apart from dharma and apart from adharma, apart from what has been done and what has not been done,
apart from what has been and what is yet to be— that which you see, tell me that.
That state which all the Vedas declare,
and which all austerities proclaim;
desiring which they lead the life of celibate studentship.
I shall declare that state to you in brief.
"Om"—this is that. 2.15.
For this indeed is the imperishable Brahman; for this indeed is the supreme imperishable.
Having known this very imperishable, whatever one desires, that belongs to him. 2.16
This is the most excellent object of focus; this is the supreme object of focus.
Having understood this object of focus, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā. || 2.17 ||
The wise one is neither born nor does he die; he has not come from anywhere, nor has anyone ever become him.
He is unborn, eternal, everlasting, and ancient.
It is not slain when the body is slain. || 2.18 ||
If the slayer thinks he slays, or if the slain thinks he is slain, they both do not understand; this one neither slays nor is slain. 2.19.
Smaller than the smallest and greater than the greatest, the Self is hidden in the cave of this living being;
one who is free from desire and devoid of sorrow beholds it.
Through the clarity of the elements, he realized his own greatness. || 2.20 ||
Seated, he goes far; lying down, he goes everywhere. Who other than myself is able to know that god who is beyond both intoxication and its absence? (2.21)
Having realized the Self—bodiless within bodies that are transient, great, and all-pervading—the wise man does not grieve. 2.22.
This Self is not to be attained by instruction,
nor by intellect, nor by much hearing;
it is attained only by him whom this Self chooses.
To him, this Self reveals its own body. 2.23.
Neither one who has not desisted from evil conduct, nor one who is not tranquil, nor one who is not concentrated, nor even one whose mind is not at peace, can attain this through wisdom. 2.24
He for whom both the Brahmin and the Kshatriya are the rice, and for whom death is the condiment—who truly knows where he is? (2.25)
Thus ends the second Vallī.
Drinking the *ṛta* in the world of good deeds, having entered the cave in the highest supreme realm,
those who know Brahman call them shadow and light.
And those who maintain the five fires and have thrice performed the Nāciketa rite. || 3.1 ||

May we be able to master the Nāciketa fire-altar—that bridge for those who have sacrificed, the imperishable Brahman which is supreme, the fearless further shore for those desiring to cross over. 3.2.
Know the self as the rider in the chariot, and the body indeed as the chariot;
know the intellect as the charioteer, and the mind as the reins. (3.3)
The wise say that the senses are the horses and the sense-objects are their paths; they say that the Self, joined with the senses and the mind, is the enjoyer. (3.4)
But for one who lacks discernment and whose mind is always undisciplined, the senses are uncontrollable, like the vicious horses of a charioteer. (3.5)
But for one who possesses discernment and whose mind is always disciplined, his senses are under control, like well-trained horses are under a charioteer. (3.6)
But he who is devoid of discernment, lacking a focused mind, and ever impure, does not attain that state and instead enters into the cycle of rebirth. (3.7)
But he who possesses discernment, who is possessed of a controlled mind and is ever pure, attains that state from which he is not born again. (3.8)
But that man who has consciousness as his charioteer and holds the reins of the mind reaches the end of the journey—that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. 3.9
For the objects are higher than the senses, and the mind is higher than the objects;
the intellect is higher than the mind, and the Great Self is higher than the intellect. 3.10
Beyond the Great is the Unmanifest; beyond the Unmanifest is the Person. There is nothing higher than the Person; that is the culmination, that is the supreme goal. 3.11.
This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth;
yet it is seen by those who perceive the subtle, through a sharp and subtle intellect. 3.12
The wise man should restrain speech and mind; he should restrain those two in the self of knowledge;
he should restrain knowledge in the Great Self, and he should restrain that in the Peaceful Self. 3.13
Arise, awake,
and having attained the boons, understand them; the edge of a razor is sharp and difficult to traverse.
The wise call that a difficult path. 3.14 ||
That which is soundless, touchless, formless, imperishable, likewise tasteless, eternal, and odorless;
which is without beginning or end, beyond the Great, and immutable.
Having realized that, one is liberated from the jaws of death. || 3.15 ||
Having recited and heard this eternal narrative of Naciketas as proclaimed by Death, the wise man is glorified in the world of Brahman.
Whoever, being self-restrained, should cause this supreme secret to be heard in an assembly of Brahmins, or at the time of a śrāddha ceremony, that leads to infinity; it leads to infinity. 3.17.
Thus ends the third Vallī.
The Self-existent pierced the openings [of the senses] outward;
therefore one looks outward, not at the inner self.
But some wise man beheld the inward self.
With his vision turned inward, desiring immortality. || 4.1 ||
Fools pursue outward desires;
they go to the snare of Death spread out. But the wise, having realized immortality, [do not].
In this world, they do not seek the permanent among things that are impermanent. || 4.2 ||
By means of this very [consciousness], one perceives form, taste, smell, sounds, and tactile objects of sexual union; what remains here [to be perceived] by another?
This indeed is that. 4.3.
The wise person does not grieve, having realized the great, all-pervading Self by which one perceives both the state of dreaming and the state of waking. 4.4
He who knows this self, the eater of honey, the living one, present nearby,
the lord of what has been and what is to be— he does not shrink away from it.
This indeed is that. 4.5.
He who was born before the heat, who was born before the waters;
he who, having entered the cave, remained there, beheld him with all beings.
This indeed is that. 4.6.
She who comes into being through the vital breath, Aditi, composed of the divine powers;
she who, having entered the secret cave, abides there and was born from all beings.
This indeed is that. 4.7.
Jātavedas is placed within the two fire-sticks,
well-nourished like an embryo by pregnant women; day after day he is to be praised by those who are watchful.
Agni [is praised] by men who possess oblations.
This indeed is that. 4.8.
From whence the sun rises and whither it sets—therein all the gods are established; no one transcends that.
This, indeed, is that. 4.9.
What is here is also there; what is there is also here. He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were multiplicity. (4.10)
This must be attained by the mind alone; there is no diversity whatsoever here. He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were diversity. (4.11)
A person the size of a thumb dwells in the center of the self;
he is the lord of what has been and what is to be, and one does not shrink away from him.
This indeed is that. 4.12.
The Person, the size of a thumb, is like a smokeless light;
he is the Lord of the past and the future; he is indeed today, and he is tomorrow.
This indeed is that. 4.13.
Just as water rained upon a mountain peak flows away in different directions, so too one who perceives dharmas as separate runs after them alone. 4.14
Just as pure water poured into pure water becomes exactly like that, so too, O Gautama, does the self of the sage who understands become. 4.15
Thus ends the fourth chapter.
Having entered the city with eleven gates belonging to the Unborn One of unswerving mind, one does not grieve; being liberated, he is set free.
This indeed is that. 5.1.
The swan dwelling in the pure, the Vasu dwelling in the mid-air, the Hotṛ dwelling on the altar, the guest dwelling in the house,
the dweller among men, the dweller in the best place, the dweller in Truth, the dweller in the sky.
Born from the lotus, born from the cow, born from the cosmic order, born from the mountain—He is the Great Cosmic Order. 5.2.
He leads the breath upward; he casts the downward breath inward.
The All-Gods worship him, the dwarf, seated in the middle. 5.3.
When this embodied being,
whose body is wasting away and who is being released from the physical frame, what remains here?
This, indeed, is that. 5.4.
No mortal lives by the out-breath (prāṇa) nor by the in-breath (apāna); rather, they live by something else upon which these two depend. 5.5
Come now, I shall declare to you this secret, eternal Brahman,
and how the self becomes [transformed] upon reaching death, O Gautama.
Some embodied beings enter a womb for the sake of a physical body; others pass into stationary objects, according to their karma and according to their learning. 5.7.
This person who remains awake while others sleep, fashioning desire after desire—that indeed is the pure, that is Brahman, that alone is called the immortal.
Upon it all worlds are supported; no one ever transcends it.
This indeed is that. 5.8.
Just as fire, though one, having entered the world, assumes a form corresponding to every form,
so too is the Inner Self of all beings one.
He assumes a form corresponding to every form, both within and without. || 5.9 ||
Just as the one wind, having entered the world, assumes a form corresponding to every form,
so too is the single inner self of all beings.
Form is the counterpart of form, both internally and externally. || 5.10 ||
Just as the sun, the eye of the entire world, is not defiled by external ocular defects,
so too is the one Inner Self of all beings.
He is not defiled by the suffering of the world, being external to it. || 5.11 ||
The one controller, the inner self of all beings, who makes his single form manifold—
those wise ones behold him abiding within themselves.
Their happiness is eternal, not that of others. || 5.12 ||
The eternal among the transient, the conscious among the conscious,
the one who ordains the desires of the many—
those wise ones behold Him dwelling within themselves.
For them there is eternal peace, but not for others. || 5.13 ||
"This is it," they think, "the supreme bliss that cannot be described.
How indeed might I know it? Does it shine, or does it blaze forth? (5.14)
There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this earthly fire.
It is only by the light of Him that everything shines.
By its light, all this shines forth. || 5.15 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter.
Rooted above and branching below is this eternal Ashvattha tree.
That alone is the Radiant, that is Brahman, and that alone is called the Immortal.
Upon it all worlds are supported; no one transcends it.
This indeed is that. 6.1.
Whatever there is in this entire world, it quivers, having issued forth from the vital breath (prāṇa).
A great terror, a raised thunderbolt—it is those who know this that become immortal. 6.2.
Out of fear of him the fire burns; out of fear the sun shines;
out of fear Indra and Vāyu, and Death as the fifth, run their course. 6.3.
If one is unable to realize this here before the dissolution of the body,
then one is subject to taking on a body again in the worlds of creation.
As it is in a mirror, so it is in the self;
as it is in a dream, so it is in the world of the ancestors;
as if clearly seen in water.
Likewise, in the world of the Gandharvas, and as with shade and sunlight in the world of Brahmā.
Having understood the distinct nature of the senses, as well as their arising and passing away, the wise man does not grieve when they arise separately. 6.6

Higher than the senses is the mind; higher than the mind is the intellect (sattva); higher than the intellect is the Great Self (mahān ātmā); and higher than the Great is the Unmanifest (avyakta). 6.7.
But beyond the unmanifest is the Puruṣa, all-pervading and indeed without marks;
by knowing him, a living being is liberated and attains immortality. (6.8)
His form does not stand within the range of vision;
no one sees him with the eye.
He is fashioned by the heart, by insight, and by the mind.
Those who know this become immortal. 6.9.
When the five senses, together with the mind, come to rest and the intellect no longer stirs, they call that the supreme state. 6.10
They consider that steady holding of the senses to be yoga; for at that time one becomes vigilant, since yoga is both the source and the dissolution [of the senses]. 6.11
It cannot be apprehended by speech, nor by mind, nor by the eye;
how else can it be perceived, other than for one who says "it exists"? (6.12)
"It exists" is how both [the self and the world] should be perceived according to their true nature;
for one who perceives them as "existing," their true nature becomes clear. (6.13)
When all desires that dwell within his heart are utterly released, then the mortal becomes immortal and attains Brahman even here. 6.14
When all the knots of the heart here on earth are rent asunder, then the mortal becomes immortal; this indeed is the extent of the instruction. 6.15.
There are one hundred and one channels of the heart; among them, one extends to the crown of the head.
Going upward by that, one attains immortality.
The others go forth in all directions at the time of departure. || 6.16 ||
The Person, the size of a thumb, is the inner self,
eternally seated in the hearts of people;
one should draw him forth from one's own body with steadfastness, as one extracts the stalk from the *muñja* grass.
One should know that as the bright, the immortal; one should know that as the bright, the immortal. 6.17.
Then Naciketas, having obtained this knowledge and the entire method of yoga as proclaimed by Death,
attained Brahman, became free from passion, and was released from death.
Any other person who would likewise direct [this] toward themselves alone [is also like this]. 6.18.
Thus ends the sixth chapter.
Thus ends the Kaṭha Upaniṣad.
